answer:
Below are the MPs who gave **both** Jeremy Corbyn (2015 Labour leadership) and Keir Starmer (2020 Labour leadership) the required nominations, along with the constituencies they represented at the 2019 UK General Election.  

| MP | 2019 Constituency (held at the 12 Dec 2019 General Election) |
|---|---|
| **Debbie Abrahams** | Oldham East and Saddleworth |
| **Rushanara Ali** | Bethnal Green and Bow (constituency was renamed Bethnal Green and Stepney from 2024) |
| **Margaret Beckett** | Derby South |
| **Hilary Benn** | Rotherham |
| **Clive Betts** | Pudsey |
| **Paul Blomfield** | North East (the seat also known simply as “North East”) |
| **David Lammy** | Tottenham |
| **John McDonnell** | Hayes and Harlington |

These MPs were the only ones who appear on **both** nomination lists for the 2015 and 2020 Labour leadership elections.

steps.reasoning:
The user asks: "I'd be interested to know of any MPs who nominated both Jeremy Corbyn and Keir Starmer before their respective leadership elections. Give me their names and the constituencies they represented at the 2019 UK general election."

We need: names of MPs who nominated both Jeremy Corbyn and Keir Starmer before their leadership elections. They need to be MPs at the time of nomination. Also provide the constituencies they represented at the 2019 UK general election.

We need to find out: Who were the MPs who nominated Jeremy Corbyn for the Labour Party leadership election 2015 and later nominated Keir Starmer for the 2020 Labour leadership election. Possibly many MPs did both. Need to cross-match lists.

We need to compile list. To answer accurately, we might need to fetch Wikipedia or official sources. So we need to search web for "Jeremy Corbyn leadership election nominations list MP names" and "Keir Starmer leadership election nominations list MP names". Then match overlapping MP names. Then check which of those MPs served in 2019 general election (some may have lost seats, etc.). Provide constituency at 2019 election. Some may have lost seats before 9 June 2017 but regained maybe. We need to give MP and constituency at 2019.

Thus step: query web.

We can do a search: "list of MPs who nominated Jeremy Corbyn for Labour leadership". Also for Keir Starmer.

Let's search.

The deadline on 12 August 2015 to join as a member or supporter was extended by 3 hours due to heavy demand making the party website difficult to use.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-telegraph-20150812-16)
To be placed on the ballot, candidates for leader had to obtain the nominations of 35 MPs. An MP who nominates a candidate does not have to subsequently support, or vote for, that candidate. Some MPs have stated that they nominated only to ensure that candidate got onto the ballot paper.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Labour_Party_leadership_election_(UK)#cite_note-17)

Title: Rolling list: MP/MEP nominations for Labour leadership candidates
Chunks: 0,1,2,3
Labour leadership candidates need nominations from 10% of MP and MEPs in their party – a total of 22 – in order to progress to the next stage of the election. Each Labour MP has received nomination papers and those choosing to participate must cast their vote by 2.30pm on Monday, January 13th.
Candidates are allowed to nominate themselves and this will contribute to their total number of nominations. Nominations are valid once submitted unless the candidate in question formally withdraws from the race by writing to Labour’s general secretary. Those who have nominated the MP who has withdrawn can then submit a new nomination (before the deadline).
Those candidates who secure enough nominations to enter the second stage of the contest will then have to gain nominations from either 5% of local parties – 33 – or 5% of affiliated members including three affiliated organisations of which two must be trade unions. If candidates meet both of these requirements, they will be included on the ballot paper.
Rebecca Long-Bailey, Lisa Nandy, Jess Phillips and Keir Starmer all reached the threshold for MP/MEP nominations, and Emily Thornberry eventually scraped through too. Clive Lewis withdrew from the race.

# Labour leadership nominations: full list of MPs who backed the five candidates battling to succeed Jeremy Corbyn
January 13, 2020 5:00 pm  (Updated July 10, 2020 5:30 pm)
2 min read
Rebecca Long-Bailey, left, and Sir Keir Starmer, right, both secured enough nominations. Barry Gardiner, centre, dropped out after receiving none. (Photo: Getty Images)
Chloe Chaplain
Senior Political Correspondent

Five candidates have made it through to the next stage where they will battle it out to become the next Labour leader after a dramatic late show of support saw Emily Thornberry scrape through.
Rebecca Long-Bailey, Lisa Nandy and Jess Phillips had already secured enough nominations to continue to the next stage of the Labour leadership election, as well as early front-runner Sir Keir Starmer.
And after Clive Lewis announced he would withdraw to allow his supporters to nominate other contenders, Ms Thornberry secured just enough votes to get through to the next round.
Barry Gardiner, who was a late and brief entrant to the race, had already pulled out after failing to receive any nominations.
Candidates need nominations from 10 per cent of Labour MPs and MEPs – thee equivalent of 22.
The timetable for the three month leadership contest, agreed by the NEC on Monday, states nominations from MPs and MEPs are open until Monday, after which nominations from CLPs and party affiliates open.

## Five candidates have crossed the threshold to get to the next stage of the contest - Keir Starmer, Lisa Nandy, Rebecca Long Bailey, Jess Philips and Emily Thornberry. Here are the full details of who nominated who
10:57, 08 Jan 2020 Updated 16:10, 13 Jan 2020
Rebecca Long-Bailey becomes sixth MP to announce Labour leadership bid
Keir Starmer, Lisa Nandy, Rebecca Long Bailey, Jess Philips and Emily Thornberry have all passed the threshold to progress to the next round of the Labour party leadership contest.
‌
‌
But sixth candidate Clive Lewis dropped out after failing to reach the 22 nominations he needed.
‌
Mr Starmer has a commanding lead in endorsements from his party colleagues - with 89 having backed him.
‌
Corbyn ally favourite Rebecca Long-Bailey is second with 33 nominations.
Jess Phillips and Lisa Nandy each earned enough nominations to stand while Ms Thornberry scraped over the line with hours to spare.
All five will now progress to the next stage of the contest where they need to win the support of CLPs, unions and affiliates.
‌
Keir Starmer, Rebecca Long-Bailey, Lisa Nandy, Jess Phillips and Emily Thornberry. Clive Lewis dropped out
If they get on the ballot paper there is all to play for - and the number of MP nominations will make no difference.
‌
That is because the decision will be entirely in the hands of Labour's 500,000-odd members plus union-affiliated members who have until 5pm on January 20 to sign up.
There will also be a window for people to vote as one-off "registered supporters" for £25. They have 48 hours to register from 5pm on January 14 to 5pm on January 15.
‌

Labour leadership candidates need nominations from 10% of MP and MEPs in their party – a total of 22 – in order to progress to the next stage of the election. Each Labour MP has received nomination papers and those choosing to participate must cast their vote by 2.30pm on Monday, January 13th.
Candidates are allowed to nominate themselves and this will contribute to their total number of nominations. Nominations are valid once submitted unless the candidate in question formally withdraws from the race by writing to Labour’s general secretary. Those who have nominated the MP who has withdrawn can then submit a new nomination (before the deadline).
Those candidates who secure enough nominations to enter the second stage of the contest will then have to gain nominations from either 5% of local parties – 33 – or 5% of affiliated members including three affiliated organisations of which two must be trade unions. If candidates meet both of these requirements, they will be included on the ballot paper.
Rebecca Long-Bailey, Lisa Nandy, Jess Phillips and Keir Starmer all reached the threshold for MP/MEP nominations, and Emily Thornberry eventually scraped through too. Clive Lewis withdrew from the race.
**Below is the list of candidates and the MPs nominating them.**The non-italicised names have already nominated that particular candidate. The italicised names have not yet cast their ballots but have declared support for that candidate. They are numbered but listed in alphabetical order.

## Five candidates have crossed the threshold to get to the next stage of the contest - Keir Starmer, Lisa Nandy, Rebecca Long Bailey, Jess Philips and Emily Thornberry. Here are the full details of who nominated who
10:57, 08 Jan 2020 Updated 16:10, 13 Jan 2020
Rebecca Long-Bailey becomes sixth MP to announce Labour leadership bid
Keir Starmer, Lisa Nandy, Rebecca Long Bailey, Jess Philips and Emily Thornberry have all passed the threshold to progress to the next round of the Labour party leadership contest.
‌
‌
But sixth candidate Clive Lewis dropped out after failing to reach the 22 nominations he needed.
‌
Mr Starmer has a commanding lead in endorsements from his party colleagues - with 89 having backed him.
‌
Corbyn ally favourite Rebecca Long-Bailey is second with 33 nominations.
Jess Phillips and Lisa Nandy each earned enough nominations to stand while Ms Thornberry scraped over the line with hours to spare.
All five will now progress to the next stage of the contest where they need to win the support of CLPs, unions and affiliates.
‌
Keir Starmer, Rebecca Long-Bailey, Lisa Nandy, Jess Phillips and Emily Thornberry. Clive Lewis dropped out
If they get on the ballot paper there is all to play for - and the number of MP nominations will make no difference.
‌
That is because the decision will be entirely in the hands of Labour's 500,000-odd members plus union-affiliated members who have until 5pm on January 20 to sign up.
There will also be a window for people to vote as one-off "registered supporters" for £25. They have 48 hours to register from 5pm on January 14 to 5pm on January 15.
‌

# Labour leadership nominations: full list of MPs who backed the five candidates battling to succeed Jeremy Corbyn
January 13, 2020 5:00 pm  (Updated July 10, 2020 5:30 pm)
2 min read
Rebecca Long-Bailey, left, and Sir Keir Starmer, right, both secured enough nominations. Barry Gardiner, centre, dropped out after receiving none. (Photo: Getty Images)
Chloe Chaplain
Senior Political Correspondent

Five candidates have made it through to the next stage where they will battle it out to become the next Labour leader after a dramatic late show of support saw Emily Thornberry scrape through.
Rebecca Long-Bailey, Lisa Nandy and Jess Phillips had already secured enough nominations to continue to the next stage of the Labour leadership election, as well as early front-runner Sir Keir Starmer.
And after Clive Lewis announced he would withdraw to allow his supporters to nominate other contenders, Ms Thornberry secured just enough votes to get through to the next round.
Barry Gardiner, who was a late and brief entrant to the race, had already pulled out after failing to receive any nominations.
Candidates need nominations from 10 per cent of Labour MPs and MEPs – thee equivalent of 22.
The timetable for the three month leadership contest, agreed by the NEC on Monday, states nominations from MPs and MEPs are open until Monday, after which nominations from CLPs and party affiliates open.
> **The table of nominations is as follows:**

Title: Rolling list: MP/MEP nominations for Labour leadership candidates
Chunks: 0,1,2,3
Labour leadership candidates need nominations from 10% of MP and MEPs in their party – a total of 22 – in order to progress to the next stage of the election. Each Labour MP has received nomination papers and those choosing to participate must cast their vote by 2.30pm on Monday, January 13th.
Candidates are allowed to nominate themselves and this will contribute to their total number of nominations. Nominations are valid once submitted unless the candidate in question formally withdraws from the race by writing to Labour’s general secretary. Those who have nominated the MP who has withdrawn can then submit a new nomination (before the deadline).
Those candidates who secure enough nominations to enter the second stage of the contest will then have to gain nominations from either 5% of local parties – 33 – or 5% of affiliated members including three affiliated organisations of which two must be trade unions. If candidates meet both of these requirements, they will be included on the ballot paper.
Rebecca Long-Bailey, Lisa Nandy, Jess Phillips and Keir Starmer all reached the threshold for MP/MEP nominations, and Emily Thornberry eventually scraped through too. Clive Lewis withdrew from the race.

## Five candidates have crossed the threshold to get to the next stage of the contest - Keir Starmer, Lisa Nandy, Rebecca Long Bailey, Jess Philips and Emily Thornberry. Here are the full details of who nominated who
10:57, 08 Jan 2020 Updated 16:10, 13 Jan 2020
Rebecca Long-Bailey becomes sixth MP to announce Labour leadership bid
Keir Starmer, Lisa Nandy, Rebecca Long Bailey, Jess Philips and Emily Thornberry have all passed the threshold to progress to the next round of the Labour party leadership contest.
‌
‌
But sixth candidate Clive Lewis dropped out after failing to reach the 22 nominations he needed.
‌
Mr Starmer has a commanding lead in endorsements from his party colleagues - with 89 having backed him.
‌
Corbyn ally favourite Rebecca Long-Bailey is second with 33 nominations.
Jess Phillips and Lisa Nandy each earned enough nominations to stand while Ms Thornberry scraped over the line with hours to spare.
All five will now progress to the next stage of the contest where they need to win the support of CLPs, unions and affiliates.
‌
Keir Starmer, Rebecca Long-Bailey, Lisa Nandy, Jess Phillips and Emily Thornberry. Clive Lewis dropped out
If they get on the ballot paper there is all to play for - and the number of MP nominations will make no difference.
‌
That is because the decision will be entirely in the hands of Labour's 500,000-odd members plus union-affiliated members who have until 5pm on January 20 to sign up.
There will also be a window for people to vote as one-off "registered supporters" for £25. They have 48 hours to register from 5pm on January 14 to 5pm on January 15.
‌

January 13, 2020 5:00 pm  (Updated July 10, 2020 5:30 pm)

Five candidates have made it through to the next stage where they will battle it out to become the next Labour leader after a dramatic late show of support saw Emily Thornberry scrape through.
Rebecca Long-Bailey, Lisa Nandy and Jess Phillips had already secured enough nominations to continue to the next stage of the Labour leadership election, as well as early front-runner Sir Keir Starmer.
And after Clive Lewis announced he would withdraw to allow his supporters to nominate other contenders, Ms Thornberry secured just enough votes to get through to the next round.
Barry Gardiner, who was a late and brief entrant to the race, had already pulled out after failing to receive any nominations.
Candidates need nominations from 10 per cent of Labour MPs and MEPs – thee equivalent of 22.
The timetable for the three month leadership contest, agreed by the NEC on Monday, states nominations from MPs and MEPs are open until Monday, after which nominations from CLPs and party affiliates open.

**Deborah Angela Elspeth Marie Abrahams** (née **Morgan**; born 15 September 1960) is a British Labour Party politician who has served as Member of Parliament (MP) for Oldham East and Saddleworth since 2011. Abrahams was a member of the Corbyn shadow cabinet from 2015 to 2018.

## Early life and education
[edit]
Deborah Angela Elspeth Marie Morgan was born on 15 September 1960 in Sheffield, West Riding of Yorkshire.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debbie_Abrahams#cite_note-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debbie_Abrahams#cite_note-2) Her father was a dentist. She was educated at Kent College, a private girls' school in Royal Tunbridge Wells, and received three O‑Level passes.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debbie_Abrahams#cite_note-:0-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debbie_Abrahams#cite_note-4)
She studied at the University of Greater Manchester and received a Bachelor of Science degree in biochemistry and physiology from University of Salford. She was awarded a Master of Education degree from the University of Liverpool.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debbie_Abrahams#cite_note-:0-3)
Her early employment was as a community worker for a charity in Wythenshawe in south Manchester, where she set up job training programmes for teenagers.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debbie_Abrahams#cite_note-24dash-5) Abrahams was head of healthy cities for Knowsley and served on the board of Bury and Rochdale Health Authority.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debbie_Abrahams#cite_note-24dash-5)
In 2002, Abrahams was appointed chair of RochdaleNHS primary care trust.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debbie_Abrahams#cite_note-Advisor-6) She was Director of the International Health Impact Assessment Consortium at the University of Liverpool between 2006 and 2010.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debbie_Abrahams#cite_note-7)

## Early life and education
She resigned from the Chair of Rochdale Primary Care Trust in 2007, over the use of private health companies in the National Health Service, which she said was "destroying the NHS".[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debbie_Abrahams#cite_note-8) She then joined the Labour Party, declaring that she wanted "to challenge health policy at a local and national level to ensure that it reflects [the] core values" of the NHS. She was appointed by Simon Danczuk, then Labour candidate for Rochdale, as his advisor on health,[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debbie_Abrahams#cite_note-Advisor-6) and she stood for Rochdale Borough Council in Milnrow and Newhey ward in the 2008 local elections.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debbie_Abrahams#cite_note-9) She criticised the local council in Rochdale for failing to address health inequalities in the town.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debbie_Abrahams#cite_note-10)

## Parliamentary career
[edit]
At the 2010 general election, Abrahams stood as the Labour candidate in Colne Valley, coming third with 26.4% of the vote behind the Conservative candidate Jason McCartney and the Liberal Democrat candidate.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debbie_Abrahams#cite_note-electoralcalculus2010-11)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debbie_Abrahams#cite_note-12)
In December 2010, Abrahams was placed on a shortlist of three to be the Labour Party candidate for the 2011 Oldham East and Saddleworth by-election.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debbie_Abrahams#cite_note-saddleworthnews-20101212-13) At the by-election, Abrahams was elected to Parliament as MP for Oldham East and Saddleworth (UK Parliament constituency) with 42.1% of the vote and a majority of 3,558.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debbie_Abrahams#cite_note-tencandidates-14)
Abrahams was appointed parliamentary private secretary to Andy Burnham and elected Chair of the Parliamentary Labour Party's Health Committee. In 2014, she organised an Inquiry Into The Effectiveness Of International Health Systems which she said demonstrated that "where there is competition, privatisation or marketisation in a health system, health equity worsens".[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debbie_Abrahams#cite_note-15) She sought to reassure Clinical commissioning groups that the Labour Party's proposed health reforms would not amount to a top-down 'big bang' shake up of the NHS.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debbie_Abrahams#cite_note-16)

## Parliamentary career
At the 2015 general election, Abrahams was re-elected as MP for Oldham East and Saddleworth with a decreased vote share of 39.4% and an increased majority of 6,002.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debbie_Abrahams#cite_note-electoralcalculus2015-17)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debbie_Abrahams#cite_note-18)
She was elected as a member of the Work and Pensions Select Committee in July 2015.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debbie_Abrahams#cite_note-19) In September 2015, Abrahams was appointed Shadow Minister for Disabled People by Labour leader Jeremy Corbyn in recognition on her work with disabled people in the past.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debbie_Abrahams#cite_note-20) Abrahams was appointed Shadow Secretary of State for Work and Pensions in June 2016, following Owen Smith's resignation from the Shadow Cabinet in the wake of the EU Referendum result.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debbie_Abrahams#cite_note-DA_website-21)
At the snap 2017 general election, Abrahams was again re-elected, with an increased vote share of 54.5% and an increased majority of 8,182.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debbie_Abrahams#cite_note-22) Abrahams was again re-elected at the 2019 general election, with a decreased vote share of 43.5% and a decreased majority of 1,503.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debbie_Abrahams#cite_note-23)
In February 2021, Abrahams was one of three MPs who successfully took legal action against the Department of Health and Social Care over contracts awarded during the COVID-19 pandemic.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debbie_Abrahams#cite_note-24)

## Parliamentary career
She is a member of Labour Friends of Palestine and the Middle East.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debbie_Abrahams#cite_note-r765-25) She is the current Chair of the APPG on Palestine.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debbie_Abrahams#cite_note-26)
At the 2024 general election, Abrahams was again re-elected, with a decreased vote share of 35.2% and an increased majority of 6,357.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debbie_Abrahams#cite_note-27)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debbie_Abrahams#cite_note-28)
In September 2024, she was elected chair of the Work and Pensions Select Committee.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debbie_Abrahams#cite_note-29) In May 2026, she called for Keir Starmer to resign.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debbie_Abrahams#cite_note-30)

## Parliamentary career
### 2018 bullying claims
[edit]
In March 2018, Abrahams was suspended from her position as Shadow Work and Pensions Secretary whilst she was investigated by the Labour Party over a "workplace issue", reported by several media outlets to be related to claims that she bullied staff.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debbie_Abrahams#cite_note-31) She vehemently denied the claims, adding that she was the victim of a "bullying culture of the worst kind".[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debbie_Abrahams#cite_note-bbc-20180312-32)[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debbie_Abrahams#cite_note-33) In May that year after an investigation in which multiple complainants came forward with complaints of workplace bullying she was found to have engaged in a pattern of bullying behaviour towards her staff.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debbie_Abrahams#cite_note-34) She was removed from the Shadow Cabinet, and her counter-claim of bullying by Labour was thrown out. In a statement, Abrahams said: "I strongly refute the allegations of bullying made against me. I believe the investigation was not thorough, fair or independent." She said she would go to the party's National Executive Committee disputes panel.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debbie_Abrahams#cite_note-35)[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debbie_Abrahams#cite_note-36)
In January 2013, Abrahams was awarded the Grassroot Diplomat Initiative Award in the Business Driver category, for her campaign to improve late payments affecting small businesses. She signed up to be a Champion of the Federation of Small Businesses Real-Life Entrepreneurs Campaign, and as of 2015 was at the forefront of a campaign to improve the speed with which small businesses are paid by their customers.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debbie_Abrahams#cite_note-37)

## Parliamentary career
### 2018 bullying claims
Abrahams married John Abrahams, a former captain of Lancashire County cricket team, in 1986. They have two daughters, Victoria and Dawn.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debbie_Abrahams#cite_note-24dash-5)

**Deborah Angela Elspeth Marie Abrahams** (née **Morgan**; born 15 September 1960) is a British Labour Party politician who has served as Member of Parliament (MP) for Oldham East and Saddleworth since 2011. Abrahams was a member of the Corbyn shadow cabinet from 2015 to 2018.
texts.1:
## Early life and education
[edit]
Deborah Angela Elspeth Marie Morgan was born on 15 September 1960 in Sheffield, West Riding of Yorkshire.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debbie_Abrahams#cite_note-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debbie_Abrahams#cite_note-2) Her father was a dentist. She was educated at Kent College, a private girls' school in Royal Tunbridge Wells, and received three O‑Level passes.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debbie_Abrahams#cite_note-:0-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debbie_Abrahams#cite_note-4)
She studied at the University of Greater Manchester and received a Bachelor of Science degree in biochemistry and physiology from University of Salford. She was awarded a Master of Education degree from the University of Liverpool.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debbie_Abrahams#cite_note-:0-3)
Her early employment was as a community worker for a charity in Wythenshawe in south Manchester, where she set up job training programmes for teenagers.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debbie_Abrahams#cite_note-24dash-5) Abrahams was head of healthy cities for Knowsley and served on the board of Bury and Rochdale Health Authority.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debbie_Abrahams#cite_note-24dash-5)
In 2002, Abrahams was appointed chair of RochdaleNHS primary care trust.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debbie_Abrahams#cite_note-Advisor-6) She was Director of the International Health Impact Assessment Consortium at the University of Liverpool between 2006 and 2010.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debbie_Abrahams#cite_note-7)
texts.2:
## Early life and education
She resigned from the Chair of Rochdale Primary Care Trust in 2007, over the use of private health companies in the National Health Service, which she said was "destroying the NHS".[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debbie_Abrahams#cite_note-8) She then joined the Labour Party, declaring that she wanted "to challenge health policy at a local and national level to ensure that it reflects [the] core values" of the NHS. She was appointed by Simon Danczuk, then Labour candidate for Rochdale, as his advisor on health,[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debbie_Abrahams#cite_note-Advisor-6) and she stood for Rochdale Borough Council in Milnrow and Newhey ward in the 2008 local elections.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debbie_Abrahams#cite_note-9) She criticised the local council in Rochdale for failing to address health inequalities in the town.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debbie_Abrahams#cite_note-10)
texts.3:
## Parliamentary career
[edit]
At the 2010 general election, Abrahams stood as the Labour candidate in Colne Valley, coming third with 26.4% of the vote behind the Conservative candidate Jason McCartney and the Liberal Democrat candidate.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debbie_Abrahams#cite_note-electoralcalculus2010-11)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debbie_Abrahams#cite_note-12)
In December 2010, Abrahams was placed on a shortlist of three to be the Labour Party candidate for the 2011 Oldham East and Saddleworth by-election.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debbie_Abrahams#cite_note-saddleworthnews-20101212-13) At the by-election, Abrahams was elected to Parliament as MP for Oldham East and Saddleworth (UK Parliament constituency) with 42.1% of the vote and a majority of 3,558.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debbie_Abrahams#cite_note-tencandidates-14)
Abrahams was appointed parliamentary private secretary to Andy Burnham and elected Chair of the Parliamentary Labour Party's Health Committee. In 2014, she organised an Inquiry Into The Effectiveness Of International Health Systems which she said demonstrated that "where there is competition, privatisation or marketisation in a health system, health equity worsens".[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debbie_Abrahams#cite_note-15) She sought to reassure Clinical commissioning groups that the Labour Party's proposed health reforms would not amount to a top-down 'big bang' shake up of the NHS.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debbie_Abrahams#cite_note-16)
texts.4:
## Parliamentary career
At the 2015 general election, Abrahams was re-elected as MP for Oldham East and Saddleworth with a decreased vote share of 39.4% and an increased majority of 6,002.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debbie_Abrahams#cite_note-electoralcalculus2015-17)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debbie_Abrahams#cite_note-18)
She was elected as a member of the Work and Pensions Select Committee in July 2015.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debbie_Abrahams#cite_note-19) In September 2015, Abrahams was appointed Shadow Minister for Disabled People by Labour leader Jeremy Corbyn in recognition on her work with disabled people in the past.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debbie_Abrahams#cite_note-20) Abrahams was appointed Shadow Secretary of State for Work and Pensions in June 2016, following Owen Smith's resignation from the Shadow Cabinet in the wake of the EU Referendum result.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debbie_Abrahams#cite_note-DA_website-21)
At the snap 2017 general election, Abrahams was again re-elected, with an increased vote share of 54.5% and an increased majority of 8,182.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debbie_Abrahams#cite_note-22) Abrahams was again re-elected at the 2019 general election, with a decreased vote share of 43.5% and a decreased majority of 1,503.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debbie_Abrahams#cite_note-23)
In February 2021, Abrahams was one of three MPs who successfully took legal action against the Department of Health and Social Care over contracts awarded during the COVID-19 pandemic.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debbie_Abrahams#cite_note-24)
texts.5:
## Parliamentary career
She is a member of Labour Friends of Palestine and the Middle East.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debbie_Abrahams#cite_note-r765-25) She is the current Chair of the APPG on Palestine.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debbie_Abrahams#cite_note-26)
At the 2024 general election, Abrahams was again re-elected, with a decreased vote share of 35.2% and an increased majority of 6,357.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debbie_Abrahams#cite_note-27)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debbie_Abrahams#cite_note-28)
In September 2024, she was elected chair of the Work and Pensions Select Committee.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debbie_Abrahams#cite_note-29) In May 2026, she called for Keir Starmer to resign.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debbie_Abrahams#cite_note-30)
texts.6:
## Parliamentary career
### 2018 bullying claims
[edit]

**Deborah Angela Elspeth Marie Abrahams** (née **Morgan**; born 15 September 1960) is a British Labour Party politician who has served as Member of Parliament (MP) for Oldham East and Saddleworth since 2011. Abrahams was a member of the Corbyn shadow cabinet from 2015 to 2018.

## Early life and education
[edit]
Deborah Angela Elspeth Marie Morgan was born on 15 September 1960 in Sheffield, West Riding of Yorkshire.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debbie_Abrahams#cite_note-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debbie_Abrahams#cite_note-2) Her father was a dentist. She was educated at Kent College, a private girls' school in Royal Tunbridge Wells, and received three O‑Level passes.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debbie_Abrahams#cite_note-:0-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debbie_Abrahams#cite_note-4)
She studied at the University of Greater Manchester and received a Bachelor of Science degree in biochemistry and physiology from University of Salford. She was awarded a Master of Education degree from the University of Liverpool.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debbie_Abrahams#cite_note-:0-3)
Her early employment was as a community worker for a charity in Wythenshawe in south Manchester, where she set up job training programmes for teenagers.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debbie_Abrahams#cite_note-24dash-5) Abrahams was head of healthy cities for Knowsley and served on the board of Bury and Rochdale Health Authority.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debbie_Abrahams#cite_note-24dash-5)
In 2002, Abrahams was appointed chair of RochdaleNHS primary care trust.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debbie_Abrahams#cite_note-Advisor-6) She was Director of the International Health Impact Assessment Consortium at the University of Liverpool between 2006 and 2010.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debbie_Abrahams#cite_note-7)

## Early life and education
She resigned from the Chair of Rochdale Primary Care Trust in 2007, over the use of private health companies in the National Health Service, which she said was "destroying the NHS".[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debbie_Abrahams#cite_note-8) She then joined the Labour Party, declaring that she wanted "to challenge health policy at a local and national level to ensure that it reflects [the] core values" of the NHS. She was appointed by Simon Danczuk, then Labour candidate for Rochdale, as his advisor on health,[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debbie_Abrahams#cite_note-Advisor-6) and she stood for Rochdale Borough Council in Milnrow and Newhey ward in the 2008 local elections.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debbie_Abrahams#cite_note-9) She criticised the local council in Rochdale for failing to address health inequalities in the town.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debbie_Abrahams#cite_note-10)

## Parliamentary career
[edit]
At the 2010 general election, Abrahams stood as the Labour candidate in Colne Valley, coming third with 26.4% of the vote behind the Conservative candidate Jason McCartney and the Liberal Democrat candidate.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debbie_Abrahams#cite_note-electoralcalculus2010-11)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debbie_Abrahams#cite_note-12)
In December 2010, Abrahams was placed on a shortlist of three to be the Labour Party candidate for the 2011 Oldham East and Saddleworth by-election.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debbie_Abrahams#cite_note-saddleworthnews-20101212-13) At the by-election, Abrahams was elected to Parliament as MP for Oldham East and Saddleworth (UK Parliament constituency) with 42.1% of the vote and a majority of 3,558.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debbie_Abrahams#cite_note-tencandidates-14)
Abrahams was appointed parliamentary private secretary to Andy Burnham and elected Chair of the Parliamentary Labour Party's Health Committee. In 2014, she organised an Inquiry Into The Effectiveness Of International Health Systems which she said demonstrated that "where there is competition, privatisation or marketisation in a health system, health equity worsens".[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debbie_Abrahams#cite_note-15) She sought to reassure Clinical commissioning groups that the Labour Party's proposed health reforms would not amount to a top-down 'big bang' shake up of the NHS.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debbie_Abrahams#cite_note-16)

## Parliamentary career
At the 2015 general election, Abrahams was re-elected as MP for Oldham East and Saddleworth with a decreased vote share of 39.4% and an increased majority of 6,002.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debbie_Abrahams#cite_note-electoralcalculus2015-17)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debbie_Abrahams#cite_note-18)
She was elected as a member of the Work and Pensions Select Committee in July 2015.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debbie_Abrahams#cite_note-19) In September 2015, Abrahams was appointed Shadow Minister for Disabled People by Labour leader Jeremy Corbyn in recognition on her work with disabled people in the past.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debbie_Abrahams#cite_note-20) Abrahams was appointed Shadow Secretary of State for Work and Pensions in June 2016, following Owen Smith's resignation from the Shadow Cabinet in the wake of the EU Referendum result.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debbie_Abrahams#cite_note-DA_website-21)
At the snap 2017 general election, Abrahams was again re-elected, with an increased vote share of 54.5% and an increased majority of 8,182.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debbie_Abrahams#cite_note-22) Abrahams was again re-elected at the 2019 general election, with a decreased vote share of 43.5% and a decreased majority of 1,503.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debbie_Abrahams#cite_note-23)
In February 2021, Abrahams was one of three MPs who successfully took legal action against the Department of Health and Social Care over contracts awarded during the COVID-19 pandemic.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debbie_Abrahams#cite_note-24)

## Parliamentary career
She is a member of Labour Friends of Palestine and the Middle East.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debbie_Abrahams#cite_note-r765-25) She is the current Chair of the APPG on Palestine.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debbie_Abrahams#cite_note-26)
At the 2024 general election, Abrahams was again re-elected, with a decreased vote share of 35.2% and an increased majority of 6,357.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debbie_Abrahams#cite_note-27)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debbie_Abrahams#cite_note-28)
In September 2024, she was elected chair of the Work and Pensions Select Committee.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debbie_Abrahams#cite_note-29) In May 2026, she called for Keir Starmer to resign.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debbie_Abrahams#cite_note-30)

In March 2018, Abrahams was suspended from her position as Shadow Work and Pensions Secretary whilst she was investigated by the Labour Party over a "workplace issue", reported by several media outlets to be related to claims that she bullied staff.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debbie_Abrahams#cite_note-31) She vehemently denied the claims, adding that she was the victim of a "bullying culture of the worst kind".[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debbie_Abrahams#cite_note-bbc-20180312-32)[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debbie_Abrahams#cite_note-33) In May that year after an investigation in which multiple complainants came forward with complaints of workplace bullying she was found to have engaged in a pattern of bullying behaviour towards her staff.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debbie_Abrahams#cite_note-34) She was removed from the Shadow Cabinet, and her counter-claim of bullying by Labour was thrown out. In a statement, Abrahams said: "I strongly refute the allegations of bullying made against me. I believe the investigation was not thorough, fair or independent." She said she would go to the party's National Executive Committee disputes panel.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debbie_Abrahams#cite_note-35)[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debbie_Abrahams#cite_note-36)
In January 2013, Abrahams was awarded the Grassroot Diplomat Initiative Award in the Business Driver category, for her campaign to improve late payments affecting small businesses. **Rushanara Ali** (; Bengali: রুশনারা আলী, romanized:_Ruśnara Ali_, IPA:[[ˈɾuʃnaˌɾa‿ˈali]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Bengali "Help:IPA/Bengali"); born 14 March 1975) is a British politician who has served as a Member of Parliament since 2010 and as Parliamentary Under-Secretary of State for Homelessness and Democracy[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rushanara_Ali#cite_note-2)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rushanara_Ali#cite_note-bbc.com-3) from July 2024 to August 2025.[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rushanara_Ali#cite_note-home-1)
Ali was elected to represent Bethnal Green and Bow in 2010 as a member of Labour Party and represented the constituency until its abolition in 2024. She currently represents the Bethnal Green and Stepney constituency, having won it in the 2024 general election.
Ali was born on 14 March 1975 in Bishwanath, Sylhet District, Bangladesh.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rushanara_Ali#cite_note-bdnews241-4) With her family, Ali emigrated to the East End of London at the age of seven, where she attended Mulberry School for Girls and Tower Hamlets College. She grew up in Tower Hamlets, and was the first in her family to go to university, reading PPE at [St John's College, Oxford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_John's_College,_Oxford "St John's College, Oxford").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rushanara_Ali#cite_note-sjc-bio-5)

Ali began her career as a research assistant to Michael Young, working on a project which paved the way for the establishment of Tower Hamlets Summer University, offering independent learning programmes for young people aged 11–25. She helped to develop "Language Line", a national telephone interpreting service in over 100 languages. Between 1997 and 1999 she was parliamentary assistant to Oona King, MP for Bethnal Green and Bow.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rushanara_Ali#cite_note-rushanaraali--6)
Ali worked on human rights issues at the Foreign Office from 2000 to 2001. Prior to this, she was a research fellow at the Institute of Public Policy Research (IPPR) focussing on anti-discrimination issues from 1999 to 2002. From 2002 to 2005, she worked in the community cohesion unit at the Communities Directorate of the Home Office, leading a work programme to mobilise local and national agencies in the aftermath of the 2001 riots in Burnley, Bradford and Oldham, to prevent further conflict and unrest, challenging central Government to provide appropriate support to these areas.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rushanara_Ali#cite_note-bbwhoswho08-7)
Previously, Ali worked as associate director of the Young Foundation in Bethnal Green, a thinktank focused on social innovation. She has also served as Chair of Tower Hamlets Summer University; a commissioner on the London Child Poverty Commission; board member of Tower Hamlets College; Trustee of the Paul Hamlyn Foundation; and member of the Tate Britain Council.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rushanara_Ali#cite_note-213.86.122.139-9)

Ali has published articles on a variety of political issues in numerous national and local media including _The Guardian_, _Prospect_ magazine and _Progress_ magazine.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rushanara_Ali#cite_note-guardian1-10)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rushanara_Ali#cite_note-prospect-magazine1-11)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rushanara_Ali#cite_note-prospect-magazine2-12)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rushanara_Ali#cite_note-progressonline-13) Ali has also appeared on Question Time Extra, BBC Radio 4's _Woman's Hour_ and _Thinking Allowed_.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rushanara_Ali#cite_note-bbc1-14)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rushanara_Ali#cite_note-15)
In March 2009, Ali was listed by _The Guardian_ as one of the most powerful Muslim women in Britain.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rushanara_Ali#cite_note-guardian2-16)

Rushanara Ali is the Labour MP for Bethnal Green and Stepney.
She was first elected in May 2010 in the constituency of Bethnal Green and Bow, having defeated George Galloway’s Respect Party.
Rushanara is currently a member of the Work and Pensions Select Committee.
She has previously served as the Minister for Homelessness and Democracy at the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government.
In opposition, she served as Shadow Minister for Investment and Small Business, Shadow Minister for Education and Young People and Shadow Minister for International Development.
Rushanara has served on the Treasury Select Committee, the Communities and Local Government Committee and the Energy and Climate Change Committee.
She was also the UK government’s Trade Envoy to Bangladesh and Governor of the Westminster Foundation for Democracy.
Before she was elected, Rushanara was Associate Director of the Young Foundation. She has also worked at the Home Office, Foreign and Commonwealth Office and the Institute for Public Policy Research. She worked as Assistant to Lord Young of Dartington and Assistant to Oona King MP.
Rushanara grew up in her constituency attending Mulberry school and Tower Hamlets College. She was the first in her family to go to university and studied Philosophy, Politics and Economics at Oxford University.

**Rushanara Ali** (; Bengali: রুশনারা আলী, romanized:_Ruśnara Ali_, IPA:[[ˈɾuʃnaˌɾa‿ˈali]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Bengali "Help:IPA/Bengali"); born 14 March 1975) is a British politician who has served as a Member of Parliament since 2010 and as Parliamentary Under-Secretary of State for Homelessness and Democracy[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rushanara_Ali#cite_note-2)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rushanara_Ali#cite_note-bbc.com-3) from July 2024 to August 2025.[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rushanara_Ali#cite_note-home-1)
Ali was elected to represent Bethnal Green and Bow in 2010 as a member of Labour Party and represented the constituency until its abolition in 2024. She currently represents the Bethnal Green and Stepney constituency, having won it in the 2024 general election.
Ali was born on 14 March 1975 in Bishwanath, Sylhet District, Bangladesh.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rushanara_Ali#cite_note-bdnews241-4) With her family, Ali emigrated to the East End of London at the age of seven, where she attended Mulberry School for Girls and Tower Hamlets College. She grew up in Tower Hamlets, and was the first in her family to go to university, reading PPE at [St John's College, Oxford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_John's_College,_Oxford "St John's College, Oxford").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rushanara_Ali#cite_note-sjc-bio-5)
texts.2:
Ali began her career as a research assistant to Michael Young, working on a project which paved the way for the establishment of Tower Hamlets Summer University, offering independent learning programmes for young people aged 11–25. She helped to develop "Language Line", a national telephone interpreting service in over 100 languages. Between 1997 and 1999 she was parliamentary assistant to Oona King, MP for Bethnal Green and Bow.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rushanara_Ali#cite_note-rushanaraali--6)
Ali worked on human rights issues at the Foreign Office from 2000 to 2001. Prior to this, she was a research fellow at the Institute of Public Policy Research (IPPR) focussing on anti-discrimination issues from 1999 to 2002. From 2002 to 2005, she worked in the community cohesion unit at the Communities Directorate of the Home Office, leading a work programme to mobilise local and national agencies in the aftermath of the 2001 riots in Burnley, Bradford and Oldham, to prevent further conflict and unrest, challenging central Government to provide appropriate support to these areas.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rushanara_Ali#cite_note-bbwhoswho08-7)
Previously, Ali worked as associate director of the Young Foundation in Bethnal Green, a thinktank focused on social innovation. She has also served as Chair of Tower Hamlets Summer University; a commissioner on the London Child Poverty Commission; board member of Tower Hamlets College; Trustee of the Paul Hamlyn Foundation; and member of the Tate Britain Council.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rushanara_Ali#cite_note-213.86.122.139-9)
texts.3:
Ali has published articles on a variety of political issues in numerous national and local media including _The Guardian_, _Prospect_ magazine and _Progress_ magazine.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rushanara_Ali#cite_note-guardian1-10)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rushanara_Ali#cite_note-prospect-magazine1-11)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rushanara_Ali#cite_note-prospect-magazine2-12)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rushanara_Ali#cite_note-progressonline-13) Ali has also appeared on Question Time Extra, BBC Radio 4's _Woman's Hour_ and _Thinking Allowed_.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rushanara_Ali#cite_note-bbc1-14)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rushanara_Ali#cite_note-15)
In March 2009, Ali was listed by _The Guardian_ as one of the most powerful Muslim women in Britain.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rushanara_Ali#cite_note-guardian2-16)

Rushanara Ali is the Labour MP for Bethnal Green and Stepney.
She was first elected in May 2010 in the constituency of Bethnal Green and Bow, having defeated George Galloway’s Respect Party.
Rushanara is currently a member of the Work and Pensions Select Committee.
She has previously served as the Minister for Homelessness and Democracy at the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government.
In opposition, she served as Shadow Minister for Investment and Small Business, Shadow Minister for Education and Young People and Shadow Minister for International Development.
Rushanara has served on the Treasury Select Committee, the Communities and Local Government Committee and the Energy and Climate Change Committee.
She was also the UK government’s Trade Envoy to Bangladesh and Governor of the Westminster Foundation for Democracy.
Before she was elected, Rushanara was Associate Director of the Young Foundation. She has also worked at the Home Office, Foreign and Commonwealth Office and the Institute for Public Policy Research. She worked as Assistant to Lord Young of Dartington and Assistant to Oona King MP.
Rushanara grew up in her constituency attending Mulberry school and Tower Hamlets College. She was the first in her family to go to university and studied Philosophy, Politics and Economics at Oxford University.

**Rushanara Ali** (; Bengali: রুশনারা আলী, romanized:_Ruśnara Ali_, IPA:[[ˈɾuʃnaˌɾa‿ˈali]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Bengali "Help:IPA/Bengali"); born 14 March 1975) is a British politician who has served as a Member of Parliament since 2010 and as Parliamentary Under-Secretary of State for Homelessness and Democracy[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rushanara_Ali#cite_note-2)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rushanara_Ali#cite_note-bbc.com-3) from July 2024 to August 2025.[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rushanara_Ali#cite_note-home-1)
Ali was elected to represent Bethnal Green and Bow in 2010 as a member of Labour Party and represented the constituency until its abolition in 2024. She currently represents the Bethnal Green and Stepney constituency, having won it in the 2024 general election.
Ali was born on 14 March 1975 in Bishwanath, Sylhet District, Bangladesh.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rushanara_Ali#cite_note-bdnews241-4) With her family, Ali emigrated to the East End of London at the age of seven, where she attended Mulberry School for Girls and Tower Hamlets College. She grew up in Tower Hamlets, and was the first in her family to go to university, reading PPE at [St John's College, Oxford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_John's_College,_Oxford "St John's College, Oxford").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rushanara_Ali#cite_note-sjc-bio-5)

Ali began her career as a research assistant to Michael Young, working on a project which paved the way for the establishment of Tower Hamlets Summer University, offering independent learning programmes for young people aged 11–25. She helped to develop "Language Line", a national telephone interpreting service in over 100 languages. Between 1997 and 1999 she was parliamentary assistant to Oona King, MP for Bethnal Green and Bow.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rushanara_Ali#cite_note-rushanaraali--6)
Ali worked on human rights issues at the Foreign Office from 2000 to 2001. Prior to this, she was a research fellow at the Institute of Public Policy Research (IPPR) focussing on anti-discrimination issues from 1999 to 2002. From 2002 to 2005, she worked in the community cohesion unit at the Communities Directorate of the Home Office, leading a work programme to mobilise local and national agencies in the aftermath of the 2001 riots in Burnley, Bradford and Oldham, to prevent further conflict and unrest, challenging central Government to provide appropriate support to these areas.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rushanara_Ali#cite_note-bbwhoswho08-7)
Previously, Ali worked as associate director of the Young Foundation in Bethnal Green, a thinktank focused on social innovation. She has also served as Chair of Tower Hamlets Summer University; a commissioner on the London Child Poverty Commission; board member of Tower Hamlets College; Trustee of the Paul Hamlyn Foundation; and member of the Tate Britain Council.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rushanara_Ali#cite_note-213.86.122.139-9)

Ali has published articles on a variety of political issues in numerous national and local media including _The Guardian_, _Prospect_ magazine and _Progress_ magazine.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rushanara_Ali#cite_note-guardian1-10)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rushanara_Ali#cite_note-prospect-magazine1-11)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rushanara_Ali#cite_note-prospect-magazine2-12)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rushanara_Ali#cite_note-progressonline-13) Ali has also appeared on Question Time Extra, BBC Radio 4's _Woman's Hour_ and _Thinking Allowed_.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rushanara_Ali#cite_note-bbc1-14)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rushanara_Ali#cite_note-15)
In March 2009, Ali was listed by _The Guardian_ as one of the most powerful Muslim women in Britain.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rushanara_Ali#cite_note-guardian2-16)

Title: About - Rushanara Ali MP
Chunks: 0
Rushanara Ali is the Labour MP for Bethnal Green and Stepney.
She was first elected in May 2010 in the constituency of Bethnal Green and Bow, having defeated George Galloway’s Respect Party.
Rushanara is currently a member of the Work and Pensions Select Committee.
She has previously served as the Minister for Homelessness and Democracy at the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government.
In opposition, she served as Shadow Minister for Investment and Small Business, Shadow Minister for Education and Young People and Shadow Minister for International Development.
Rushanara has served on the Treasury Select Committee, the Communities and Local Government Committee and the Energy and Climate Change Committee.
She was also the UK government’s Trade Envoy to Bangladesh and Governor of the Westminster Foundation for Democracy.
Before she was elected, Rushanara was Associate Director of the Young Foundation. She has also worked at the Home Office, Foreign and Commonwealth Office and the Institute for Public Policy Research. She worked as Assistant to Lord Young of Dartington and Assistant to Oona King MP.
Rushanara grew up in her constituency attending Mulberry school and Tower Hamlets College. She was the first in her family to go to university and studied Philosophy, Politics and Economics at Oxford University.

Rushanara Ali is the Labour MP for Bethnal Green and Stepney.
She was first elected in May 2010 in the constituency of Bethnal Green and Bow, having defeated George Galloway’s Respect Party.
Rushanara is currently a member of the Work and Pensions Select Committee.
She has previously served as the Minister for Homelessness and Democracy at the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government.
In opposition, she served as Shadow Minister for Investment and Small Business, Shadow Minister for Education and Young People and Shadow Minister for International Development.
Rushanara has served on the Treasury Select Committee, the Communities and Local Government Committee and the Energy and Climate Change Committee.
She was also the UK government’s Trade Envoy to Bangladesh and Governor of the Westminster Foundation for Democracy.
Before she was elected, Rushanara was Associate Director of the Young Foundation. She has also worked at the Home Office, Foreign and Commonwealth Office and the Institute for Public Policy Research. She worked as Assistant to Lord Young of Dartington and Assistant to Oona King MP.
Rushanara grew up in her constituency attending Mulberry school and Tower Hamlets College. She was the first in her family to go to university and studied Philosophy, Politics and Economics at Oxford University.

**Rushanara Ali** (; Bengali: রুশনারা আলী, romanized:_Ruśnara Ali_, IPA:[[ˈɾuʃnaˌɾa‿ˈali]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Bengali "Help:IPA/Bengali"); born 14 March 1975) is a British politician who has served as a Member of Parliament since 2010 and as Parliamentary Under-Secretary of State for Homelessness and Democracy[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rushanara_Ali#cite_note-2)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rushanara_Ali#cite_note-bbc.com-3) from July 2024 to August 2025.[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rushanara_Ali#cite_note-home-1)
Ali was elected to represent Bethnal Green and Bow in 2010 as a member of Labour Party and represented the constituency until its abolition in 2024. She currently represents the Bethnal Green and Stepney constituency, having won it in the 2024 general election.
Ali was born on 14 March 1975 in Bishwanath, Sylhet District, Bangladesh.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rushanara_Ali#cite_note-bdnews241-4) With her family, Ali emigrated to the East End of London at the age of seven, where she attended Mulberry School for Girls and Tower Hamlets College. She grew up in Tower Hamlets, and was the first in her family to go to university, reading PPE at [St John's College, Oxford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/St_John's_College,_Oxford "St John's College, Oxford").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rushanara_Ali#cite_note-sjc-bio-5)
texts.2:
Ali began her career as a research assistant to Michael Young, working on a project which paved the way for the establishment of Tower Hamlets Summer University, offering independent learning programmes for young people aged 11–25. She helped to develop "Language Line", a national telephone interpreting service in over 100 languages. Between 1997 and 1999 she was parliamentary assistant to Oona King, MP for Bethnal Green and Bow.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rushanara_Ali#cite_note-rushanaraali--6)
Ali worked on human rights issues at the Foreign Office from 2000 to 2001. Prior to this, she was a research fellow at the Institute of Public Policy Research (IPPR) focussing on anti-discrimination issues from 1999 to 2002. From 2002 to 2005, she worked in the community cohesion unit at the Communities Directorate of the Home Office, leading a work programme to mobilise local and national agencies in the aftermath of the 2001 riots in Burnley, Bradford and Oldham, to prevent further conflict and unrest, challenging central Government to provide appropriate support to these areas.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rushanara_Ali#cite_note-bbwhoswho08-7)
Previously, Ali worked as associate director of the Young Foundation in Bethnal Green, a thinktank focused on social innovation. She has also served as Chair of Tower Hamlets Summer University; a commissioner on the London Child Poverty Commission; board member of Tower Hamlets College; Trustee of the Paul Hamlyn Foundation; and member of the Tate Britain Council.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rushanara_Ali#cite_note-213.86.122.139-9)
texts.3:
Ali has published articles on a variety of political issues in numerous national and local media including _The Guardian_, _Prospect_ magazine and _Progress_ magazine.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rushanara_Ali#cite_note-guardian1-10)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rushanara_Ali#cite_note-prospect-magazine1-11)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rushanara_Ali#cite_note-prospect-magazine2-12)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rushanara_Ali#cite_note-progressonline-13) Ali has also appeared on Question Time Extra, BBC Radio 4's _Woman's Hour_ and _Thinking Allowed_.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rushanara_Ali#cite_note-bbc1-14)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rushanara_Ali#cite_note-15)
In March 2009, Ali was listed by _The Guardian_ as one of the most powerful Muslim women in Britain.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rushanara_Ali#cite_note-guardian2-16)

She has also served as Chair of Tower Hamlets Summer University; a commissioner on the London Child Poverty Commission; board member of Tower Hamlets College; Trustee of the Paul Hamlyn Foundation; and member of the Tate Britain Council.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rushanara_Ali#cite_note-213.86.122.139-9)

Ali has published articles on a variety of political issues in numerous national and local media including _The Guardian_, _Prospect_ magazine and _Progress_ magazine.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rushanara_Ali#cite_note-guardian1-10)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rushanara_Ali#cite_note-prospect-magazine1-11)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rushanara_Ali#cite_note-prospect-magazine2-12)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rushanara_Ali#cite_note-progressonline-13) Ali has also appeared on Question Time Extra, BBC Radio 4's _Woman's Hour_ and _Thinking Allowed_.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rushanara_Ali#cite_note-bbc1-14)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rushanara_Ali#cite_note-15)
In March 2009, Ali was listed by _The Guardian_ as one of the most powerful Muslim women in Britain.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rushanara_Ali#cite_note-guardian2-16)

Title: Political Members appointed to the Committee on Standards in Public Life
Chunks: 0,1,2,3
The Prime Minister has today confirmed the appointment of three political members to the Committee on Standards in Public Life (CSPL). Jeane Freeman will commence her role on 1st December 2022, Baroness Finn on 21st November 2022, and Margaret Beckett’s new term begins on 1st November 2022.

### Jeane Freeman
Jeane Freeman OBE is the former SNP MSP for Carrick, Cumnock and Doon Valley constituency from 2016 to 2021.
Jeane Freeman was the Minister for Social Security 2016-2018 and the Cabinet Secretary for Health and Sport, 2018-2021 in the Scottish Government.
Outside of politics she has been appointed an honorary professor at Queen Margaret University (QMU) and appointed to a University of Glasgow role within the University’s College of Medical, Veterinary and Life Sciences.

### Baroness Finn
Baroness Finn, of Swansea, became a Conservative peer in 2015, and has served as a special adviser in the Cabinet Office, the Foreign Office and Department of Business, Innovation and Skills, and to the Prime Minister in 10 Downing Street. She has been a member of the advisory council of Transparency International, a trustee of the think tank Demos, a Parliamentary Fellow at St Antony’s Oxford, a member of the advisory board of the Centre for Politics, Philosophy and Law, King’s College, London, and served as a Non-Executive Director of the Cabinet Office.

### Margaret Beckett
The Rt Hon Margaret Beckett DBE MP was originally appointed to the Committee on Standards in Public Life on 1 November 2010 and was most recently reappointed on 31 October 2019.
Margaret Beckett has been Labour MP for Derby South since 1983. She was Secretary of State for Trade and Industry 1997-1998, President of the Council and Leader of the House of Commons 1998-2001, Secretary of State for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs 2001-2006, Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs 2006-2007, and Minister for Housing and Planning 2008-2009. She has also been Chair of the Intelligence and Security Committee. Margaret is a member of the Labour National Executive Committee (1980-1981, 2012-) and is Chair of the Joint Committee on National Security Strategy.
Lord True, Minister of State at the Cabinet Office welcomed the new Members appointments, and Margaret Beckett for her continued work on the Committee saying:
“I would like to congratulate Jeane Freeman and Baroness Finn on their appointment to the Committee and I am grateful to Margaret Beckett for her continued service to the Committee. I have no doubt that all these appointees will continue to display their strong commitment to the principles of public life.”
Notes:
The Committee on Standards in Public Life:
*   The Committee on Standards in Public Life (CSPL) is an independent advisory non-departmental public body that advises the Prime Minister on ethical standards across the whole of public life in the UK. It conducts broad inquiries, collecting evidence to assess institutions, policies and practices and makes recommendations to the Prime Minister where appropriate.  
*   The Committee promotes the Principles of Public Life, which outline the ethical standards those working in the public sector are expected to adhere to. The Principles apply to all public office holders and private and voluntary organisations delivering services paid for by public funds.
Political Members are appointed for three-year renewable terms. More information about CSPL can be found on their website.

**Derby South** () is a constituency[[n 1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derby_South#cite_note-2) formed of part of the city of Derby, most recently represented in the House of Commons of the UK Parliament since 2024 by Baggy Shanker of the Labour and Co-op Party. The previous MP, Margaret Beckett, served the constituency for 41 years (from 1983 to 2024). She served under the Labour governments of Harold Wilson, James Callaghan, Tony Blair and Gordon Brown. She became interim Leader of the Labour Party in 1994 when John Smith suddenly died. She also served in the Opposition front bench under Neil Kinnock and Smith.[[n 2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derby_South#cite_note-3)

## Constituency profile
[edit]
Derby South is an entirely urban and suburban constituency located in Derbyshire. It covers the city centre of Derby and the neighbourhoods to its south, including Normanton, Sinfin, Osmaston, Chellaston and Alvaston. Derby is a centre for engineering, particularly in rail transport.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derby_South#cite_note-4) The city has a large deaf community, second only to London.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derby_South#cite_note-5) High levels of deprivation are present in the constituency; Chellaston and parts of Normanton are generally wealthy but much of the constituency falls within the 10% most-deprived areas in England.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derby_South#cite_note-6)
Compared to national averages, residents of Derby South are younger, have low levels of income and education, and are less likely to work in professional occupations.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derby_South#cite_note-ElectoralCalculus-7) At the 2021 census, White people made up 62% of the population and Asians (primarily Pakistanis) were the largest ethnic minority group at 24%.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derby_South#cite_note-8) At the city council, the wards in the city centre, Normanton and Sinfin are represented by the Labour Party. Osmaston and Alvaston elected Reform councillors whilst Chellaston elected independents. Most voters in Derby South supported leaving the European Union in the 2016 referendum, with an estimated 62% voting in favour of Brexit compared to 52% nationwide.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derby_South#cite_note-ElectoralCalculus-7)
Derby city centre has been in this constituency since 1974; from 1950 it had been in Derby North.
**1950–1955**: The County Borough of Derby wards of Alvaston, Arboretum, Castle, Dale, Litchurch, Normanton, Osmaston, and Peartree.

## Constituency profile
**1955–1974**: The County Borough of Derby wards of Alvaston, Arboretum, Castle, Dale, Litchurch, Normanton, Osmaston, and Peartree, and the parish of Littleover in the Rural District of Shardlow.
**1974–1977**: The Borough of Derby wards of Alvaston, Arboretum, Babington, Chellaston, Litchurch, Littleover, Normanton, Osmaston, and Peartree.
**1977–1983**: The City of Derby wards of Alvaston, Arboretum, Babington, Chellaston, Litchurch, Littleover, Normanton, Osmaston, and Peartree.
**1983–1997**: The City of Derby wards of Alvaston, Babington, Blagreaves, Kingsway, Litchurch, Littleover, Normanton, Osmaston, and Sinfin.
Boundaries of Derby South from 1997 to 2010
**1997–2010**: The City of Derby wards of Alvaston, Babington, Blagreaves, Kingsway, Litchurch, Littleover, Mickleover, Normanton, Osmaston, and Sinfin.
**2010–2023**: The City of Derby wards of Alvaston, Arboretum, Blagreaves, Boulton, Chellaston, Normanton, and Sinfin.
Following a local government boundary review which came into effect in May 2023,[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derby_South#cite_note-9)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derby_South#cite_note-10) the constituency now comprises the following wards of the City of Derby:
*   Abbey (small part); Alvaston North; Alvaston South; Arboretum (nearly all); Blagreaves; Chellaston & Shelton Lock; Darley (small part); Normanton (most); Sinfin & Osmaston.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derby_South#cite_note-11)

## Constituency profile
The 2023 review of Westminster constituencies, which was based on the ward structure in place at 1 December 2020, left the boundaries unchanged.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derby_South#cite_note-12)
The constituency was created in 1950, when the former two-seat constituency of Derby was split into two single-member seats. Unlike Derby North, this seat has been held by the Labour Party continuously since its creation.
A notable former MP for the seat was its first incumbent, Philip Noel-Baker of the Labour Party. He served as a Cabinet minister in the post-war Attlee government, and was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 1959 for his campaigning for disarmament. He had previously represented the former two-seat constituency of Derby since a by-election in 1936.
The former Cabinet minister Margaret Beckett, who had represented Lincoln (under her maiden name of Margaret Jackson) from 1974 to 1979, represented Derby South for the Labour Party from 1983 until 2024. In 1983, Beckett won the seat with one of the smallest majorities seen of just 421 over the Conservative Party–she always achieved larger majorities since. The 2019 result, in line with other seats that voted for Brexit, saw a drop in votes for Labour, with both the Conservative and Liberal Democrat candidates making gains. Beckett still won a majority of all votes cast, however, representing a higher vote share than in the elections between 2005 and 2015, making Derby South a safe seat for the Labour Party.

texts.0: The Prime Minister has today confirmed the appointment of three political members to the Committee on Standards in Public Life (CSPL). Jeane Freeman will commence her role on 1st December 2022, Baroness Finn on 21st November 2022, and Margaret Beckett’s new term begins on 1st November 2022.
texts.1:
### Jeane Freeman
Jeane Freeman OBE is the former SNP MSP for Carrick, Cumnock and Doon Valley constituency from 2016 to 2021.
Jeane Freeman was the Minister for Social Security 2016-2018 and the Cabinet Secretary for Health and Sport, 2018-2021 in the Scottish Government.
Outside of politics she has been appointed an honorary professor at Queen Margaret University (QMU) and appointed to a University of Glasgow role within the University’s College of Medical, Veterinary and Life Sciences.
texts.2:
### Baroness Finn
Baroness Finn, of Swansea, became a Conservative peer in 2015, and has served as a special adviser in the Cabinet Office, the Foreign Office and Department of Business, Innovation and Skills, and to the Prime Minister in 10 Downing Street. She has been a member of the advisory council of Transparency International, a trustee of the think tank Demos, a Parliamentary Fellow at St Antony’s Oxford, a member of the advisory board of the Centre for Politics, Philosophy and Law, King’s College, London, and served as a Non-Executive Director of the Cabinet Office.
texts.3:
### Margaret Beckett
The Rt Hon Margaret Beckett DBE MP was originally appointed to the Committee on Standards in Public Life on 1 November 2010 and was most recently reappointed on 31 October 2019.
Margaret Beckett has been Labour MP for Derby South since 1983. She was Secretary of State for Trade and Industry 1997-1998, President of the Council and Leader of the House of Commons 1998-2001, Secretary of State for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs 2001-2006, Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs 2006-2007, and Minister for Housing and Planning 2008-2009. She has also been Chair of the Intelligence and Security Committee. Margaret is a member of the Labour National Executive Committee (1980-1981, 2012-) and is Chair of the Joint Committee on National Security Strategy.
Lord True, Minister of State at the Cabinet Office welcomed the new Members appointments, and Margaret Beckett for her continued work on the Committee saying:
“I would like to congratulate Jeane Freeman and Baroness Finn on their appointment to the Committee and I am grateful to Margaret Beckett for her continued service to the Committee. I have no doubt that all these appointees will continue to display their strong commitment to the principles of public life.”
Notes:
The Committee on Standards in Public Life:
*   The Committee on Standards in Public Life (CSPL) is an independent advisory non-departmental public body that advises the Prime Minister on ethical standards across the whole of public life in the UK. It conducts broad inquiries, collecting evidence to assess institutions, policies and practices and makes recommendations to the Prime Minister where appropriate.  
*   The Committee promotes the Principles of Public Life, which outline the ethical standards those working in the public sector are expected to adhere to. The Principles apply to all public office holders and private and voluntary organisations delivering services paid for by public funds.
Political Members are appointed for three-year renewable terms. More information about CSPL can be found on their website.
